anchors.fact: In April 1843 the fortress of Perote, Mexico, held prisoners from Texas taken in the 1842 raids each way: about fifty Bexar men, captured when Woll's army seized San Antonio on 11 September 1842 (Green pp. 29–30, 39, 235; App. I p. 447; TSHA "Perote Prison"), Trimble among them (App. I p. 448); and Green with fifteen Mier men, taken after the Texan raid on Mier in December 1842 (pp. 74–82, 243; TSHA "Mier Expedition"). All hands came to the bowl (p. 259). They were months from home ("five months" is the Mier party's figure, p. 256), in chains, in cold quarters (pp. 256–258; F2–F3, C5).
anchors.meaning: A hardship that lasted: the long middle, not one bad day. They weren't innocents: men taken in raids both ways, told once and without a side.
anchors.speaksTo: one true thing: still funny on the fortieth day; limb 1

anchors.fact: They stood round their bowl in rags with chains riveted on their ankles, which they called their "jewelry" (Green p. 259, F7).
anchors.meaning: The room's own refusal, in one word.

anchors.fact: For their celebration they bought mezcal ("vino mascal"), ass's milk, thirty dozen eggs and a loaf of sugar, and used all their cooking utensils and water jars to make egg-nog; three officers beat the eggs, another pounded the sugar (Green p. 259, F5–F6).
anchors.meaning: The drink is on the same page as the joke.

anchors.fact: Their shouts alarmed the guards, who feared a riot; the captain of the guard came round to know the cause, was answered, said "Bueno" and started to go (Green p. 260, F9).
anchors.meaning: The threat walks in on the one good evening.
anchors.speaksTo: fear: the bad thing showing through

anchors.fact: Then they gave the wink to Trimble, who could mimic an owl: he rolled his eyes over, twisted his head "clean round" and whooped. The captain turned, frowned, hesitated whether to laugh or swear, said "Tecolote" (screech-owl) and moved on, to a roar of laughter from the room (Green pp. 260–261, F10). Told by a witness who wrote it down in 1845: "as he tells it".
anchors.meaning: Make the threat a little ridiculous; the threat itself names the joke.
anchors.speaksTo: one true thing; method: make it ridiculous; limb 3–4; everyone checks their face

anchors.fact: The nickname stayed with Trimble to his grave (Green p. 261, F11).
anchors.meaning: The mark: the others repeated the joke.
anchors.speaksTo: driver: LEAVE A MARK; bonus limb

anchors.fact: At a later roll call, "Tecolote" delivered the cover line for two men lying on the floor ("Here is two muy malo"), "with an admirable mixture of confidence and sympathy", and the officer left. The line was the group's plan; the delivery was his, with a straight face (Green pp. 314–315, F12).
anchors.meaning: The same nerve without the laugh: being there for others.
anchors.speaksTo: position: on the day the joke won't come, turn up anyway; gives: dignity in the middle of it

anchors.fact: Another night, the sentinel at their door was made good-natured with mezcal passed through the grates in an eggshell: nothing larger could pass (Green p. 316, F13).
anchors.meaning: Even the man guarding the door got a sip: the half-shell beside the cup.
anchors.speaksTo: the drink's touch; joke on the situation, never on the guard

anchors.fact: Eggnog is on record from 1788 (Oxford EGGNOG pdf 702; *Imbibe!* pdf 127); the *Codex* calls it "the classic example" of egg with dairy (p. 256); the classic ends with nutmeg (*Codex* p. 256; Oxford pdf 703). A mezcal egg-nog is on record (*Imbibe!* pdf 127). Ours: joven mezcal, whole egg, cow's milk for the ass's milk, rich syrup for the sugar loaf, no nutmeg because none was on their list (p. 259).
anchors.meaning: A renowned classic, made from their list. Never "their recipe": the milk and syrup are ours.

cocktail.closingLine: Fill the shell for whoever's on watch. On the days nothing's funny, show up all the same.
cocktail.glassware: a small plain earthenware cup (about 300 ml), chilled in the freezer; any small tumbler will do
method: Put the cup in the freezer for ten minutes. Make the syrup ahead: stir two parts sugar into one part warm water, by weight, until it's clear, then let it cool.
Wash the egg. Crack it cleanly into the shaker, keeping one half of the shell whole, and rinse that half under the tap.
Add the mezcal, the milk and the syrup.
Shake hard without ice for about fifteen seconds. That beats the egg, which was the job three of them did by hand.
Add ice and shake again, hard and loud, for about twelve seconds.
Strain it into the cold cup. Nothing goes on top: no nutmeg, no cinnamon.
Stand the half-shell up beside the cup and pour a teaspoon of mezcal into it.
cocktail.name: The Wink

recipe.note: any unaged mezcal of 40% or stronger; no particular village needed
wash it before you crack it, because half its shell gets used. It's raw, so use a pasteurised egg if the drink is for anyone pregnant, elderly or unwell
theirs was donkey's milk. Use milk, not cream, so it stays light
for their loaf of sugar: two parts sugar to one of water, by weight, stirred until clear

recipe.item: more mezcal, in half the eggshell
recipe.note: not in the drink: it's for someone else

cocktail.tagline: Things get bad. You get funnier.

reading.epigraph: Mezcal, eggs and milk, once mixed in prisoners' water jars. Nobody stopped them.
whoYouAre: It's been bad for a while now. Not one bad day: weeks of it, the kind where everyone has run out of things to say. And you're still funny. Not loud, just there every morning with something, the way some people bring coffee. When it gets worse, people glance at you before they decide how worried to be.

People say nothing gets to you. It all gets to you. You've just decided it doesn't get the last word. What you don't mention is that each day the next joke takes a little more finding, and that you sometimes wonder about the morning nothing comes, when everyone looking at your face sees what you've been holding off. And what you give them is the thing they need most: while someone's still laughing, they're still themselves, not just people something is happening to.
yours: In April 1843, the fortress prison at Perote, in Mexico, held prisoners from Texas: men taken in the raids the two had been making on each other the year before, months from home now, with chains riveted round their ankles. They called the chains their jewellery. For a date that mattered to them, they got hold of mezcal, eggs, donkey's milk and a loaf of sugar, and made eggnog with every cooking utensil and water jar they had.

It got loud enough that the guards feared a riot. Their captain came round, was told it was how the prisoners kept their saints' days at home, and turned to go. That's when they gave the wink to a man called Trimble, who could do an owl. He rolled his eyes right back, twisted his head clean round and whooped. As one prisoner's journal tells it, the captain turned, frowned, and couldn't decide whether to laugh or swear. Then he said "Tecolote", screech-owl, and walked on, with the whole room roaring behind him. The name stuck to Trimble for good.

Everybody there knew whose face to turn to. The owl didn't make the chains any lighter. It let a roomful of prisoners be themselves for a minute, inside a fortress's walls, and even the captain who'd come to find out what the noise was ended up naming the joke. Later, at a roll call, it was Tecolote who covered for two of the others lying on the floor, sure of himself and kind with it, with a straight face. I like to think it was the same nerve the owl was made of. That's you: the laugh and the nerve, from the same place.

The cocktail I've made for you is that eggnog, made for one: joven mezcal, a whole egg, whole milk in place of the donkey's, and sugar, shaken until it's light and thick. Eggnog itself is a classic, on record since 1788, and the classic ends with nutmeg grated on top. This one doesn't, because there was none on their list: nothing goes in that wasn't on it. Crack the egg cleanly before you shake, keep half the shell, rinse it, and when the drink is poured, put a teaspoon of mezcal in it. On another night at Perote, the prisoners kept the guard at their door in a good mood with a sip of mezcal passed through the bars in an eggshell, because nothing bigger would fit. I kept the shell as a nod to that: even the man guarding the door got a sip.

Some day the joke won't come. That isn't the day it wins. On the morning you've got nothing, let it not come. Go in anyway, unfunny, and just be there. My guess is that on that morning someone else will find the joke for once, because you've been showing them how every day. I'd love you to be there to laugh at it.
